newsitem.title: CYPRUS: FEATURE-Cyprus prays for deluge to end drought.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Cyprus prays for deluge to end drought.

text.p: The reservoir in the foothills of Pharmakas village has been reduced to a muddy puddle of moss-green water, a measuring rod sticking out starkly from its middle.
Further up, the hills are densely covered with tomato plantations, so far unaffected by the prolonged drought that has stricken the eastern Mediterranean island.
While Europe shivers from its coldest weather in decades, sun-soaked Cyprus is literally praying for divine intervention to end the long spell of low rainfall.
"We believe that if we join in prayer to our Virtuous Heavenly Father with a warm soul and deep faith, He cannot but hear us and respond to our request," an Orthodox Church circular said.
Spring-like temperatures have averaged two degrees above normal levels of 17 Celsius (62.5 Fahrenheit) since mid-December in the capital Nicosia, where days of glorious sunshine seem endless.
Like the Pharmakas reservoir, one of the smallest on the island, other water reserves are depleting at an alarming pace as authorities desperately search for ways to save water.
"The situation can only be described as tragic," said Lakis Christodoulou, director of the water development department at the Agriculture Ministry. "The recent rain we had did not help things."
Farmers will have to be rationed if the drought does not end soon.
Daily checks have shown that the 17 largest reservoirs are only 20 percent full. None passed the half-full mark in 1996.
LOOKING FOR ALTERNATIVES

Water is becoming a rarer and rarer commodity as rain, the only source on Cyprus, appears nowhere in sight and demand from the 700,000 inhabitants and two million tourists who visit each year is surging.

After toying with different ideas of how to solve the shortage -- even including one suggestion to import water in balloons from Crete -- the authorities went back to the more conventional option of desalination.
A desalination plant being built at a cost of $25 million is due to come on stream in the southeast of the island in April.
The plant, built by a private company under a build-operate-transfer contract, will sell desalinated water to the government for 10 years and will then become the property of the government.
The plant will have an output of about 25,000 cubic metres (over 880,000 cubic feet) a day, a fifth of the total channelled on the central distribution system.
But that meets only half the daily needs of Nicosia.

"We have proposed (to the government) an extension of the capacity of the desalination plant by 50 percent and to build a second plant with an output of 20,000 cubic metres (about 700,000 cubic feet) per day," said Christodoulou.
SAVING THROUGH PUBLIC AWARENESS
The water development department is campaigning to drum a "water-saving conscience" into Cypriots.

Strict laws enacted during the previous serious drought, in 1991, make it a criminal offence to use a hose to wash a vehicle or pavement. Those caught are liable a 300 pound ($650) fine or three months in jail.
Nevertheless, hosing cars, pavements, balconies -- sometimes even the street outside the front door -- is still a national pastime on Sunday mornings.
More than two hundred people have been fined since last June, when the most recent water-saving campaign started.
"Some people act as though we always have plenty of rain," Christodoulou said.
Last year authorities restricted supplies to regional distribution boards by 10 percent.
Water for seasonal crops was slashed between 30 and 40 percent and for conventional crops by 25 percent.
Seasonal crops could face the chop soon as the government ponders scrapping supplies there altogether.
"Many farmers use boreholes but it is expensive and there are not many reserves," said farmer's union representative Costas Constantinides.
"We are getting desperate."
($=0.46 Cyprus pounds)
